title: Directory Structures & Mounting
summary: How directories organize names into a navigable tree, how paths resolve component by component, and how separate file systems get grafted into one namespace via mounting.

slides.markdown:
A directory is a special file whose content is a table of name-to-inode mappings ([Inodes & Unix File Systems](inodes-and-unix-file-systems)). Chain enough of these tables together and you get a tree — the single namespace you navigate with `cd` and `ls`.

This topic covers two things that look unrelated but aren't: how a path like `/a/b/c.txt` actually resolves component by component, and how **mounting** lets an entirely separate disk or network share appear as just another directory in that same tree, with no visible seam.

slides.sectionTitle: Directories as a special file: a table of mappings
slides.markdown:
A directory's data blocks hold entries of the form `(name, inode number)` — nothing more. `ls` reads this table and, for `ls -l`, follows each inode number to fetch metadata for display. Two entries every directory has by convention: `.` (its own inode number) and `..` (its parent's inode number) — which is why `cd ..` works purely by following a stored pointer, no path-string arithmetic required.

Because a directory is just a file, it has its own inode, its own size (which grows as you add entries), and can itself be a target of `stat`.

The earliest file systems used a **single-level directory** — every file in the entire system in one flat list. It fails almost immediately at any scale: two users (or two projects) can't both have a file named `notes.txt`, and there's no way to organize related files together.

**Tree-structured directories** fix this by letting any directory contain subdirectories, giving each a unique **path** even when the leaf name repeats — `/alice/notes.txt` and `/bob/notes.txt` coexist without conflict. Every general-purpose OS today uses a tree; single-level survives only in deliberately minimal contexts (an old CP/M floppy, a tiny embedded flash chip).

slides.sectionTitle: Absolute vs relative paths and path resolution
slides.markdown:
An **absolute path** starts from the root (`/etc/nginx/nginx.conf`) and resolves the same way regardless of your current location. A **relative path** (`../config/nginx.conf`) resolves starting from the process's **current working directory**, tracked per-process in the kernel and changed by `chdir()` (what `cd` calls).

Resolution is always component-by-component: the kernel starts at either root or the cwd's inode, then for each path segment looks up that name in the current directory's entry table to get the next inode, repeating until the path is exhausted. `.` and `..` are handled the same way — as ordinary lookups against entries every directory already has.

![path resolution lookups for /a/b/c.txt](assets/path-resolution-lookups.svg)

Each arrow in this diagram is one directory read plus one lookup — resolving `/a/b/c.txt` costs three lookups minimum, one per path component, each requiring the previous directory's inode to already be resolved.

This is exactly why the kernel's dentry (directory entry) cache matters: without it, every `open()` on a deep path would re-walk every component from root, hitting disk repeatedly for data that rarely changes.

slides.sectionTitle: Mount points: grafting one file system onto another's tree
slides.markdown:
A **mount point** is an existing directory that, after `mount(device, dir)`, transparently becomes the root of a *different* file system — a separate disk partition, a USB drive, an NFS share, or a tmpfs RAM disk. Once mounted, walking into that directory silently crosses into the other file system's own inode table; the path syntax shows no seam at all.

```bash
$ mount /dev/sdb1 /mnt/backup
$ ls /mnt/backup        # now listing sdb1's root directory
$ df -T /mnt/backup      # confirms which filesystem and device is mounted there
```

Before the mount, `/mnt/backup` was just an empty directory on the root file system; after, everything under it belongs to `/dev/sdb1` until it's unmounted.

slides.sectionTitle: Why Unix has one tree while Windows uses drive letters
slides.markdown:
| | Unix (single tree) | Windows (drive letters) |
|---|---|---|
| Namespace | One tree from `/`; other file systems mount into it at any directory | Each volume gets its own root — `C:\`, `D:\` — separate namespaces |
| Adding storage | Mount at any existing path, invisibly | Assign a new drive letter |
| Path portability | A path like `/mnt/data/x` doesn't reveal which physical device | `D:\x` explicitly names the volume |
| Moving a mount | Just remount elsewhere — paths above the mount point are unaffected | Changing a drive letter can break every reference to it |

**How to decide:** the Unix model trades explicitness (you can't tell which physical device a path lives on just by reading it) for flexibility — storage can be added, moved, or reorganized without every application's hardcoded paths breaking.

slides.sectionTitle: What actually happens across a mount boundary
slides.markdown:
Crossing a mount point means every subsequent lookup uses a *different* inode table, and — critically — inode numbers are no longer comparable across the boundary. Two files with the same inode number on different mounted file systems are unrelated; this is precisely why hard links can't cross mount points, even if both are technically "under `/`."

Unmounting (`umount`) requires nothing on that file system to be in use — an open file, a process with its cwd there, or another mount nested inside will all cause `umount` to fail with `EBUSY` until they're cleared, which is why `lsof +D /mnt/x` is the standard first debugging step for a stuck unmount.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: a path resolution failing partway
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "If `open("/a/b/c.txt")` fails, it means `c.txt` doesn't exist."

**Why it's wrong:** resolution fails at the *first* component it can't process, and the reason varies by which component and why: `a` might not exist (`ENOENT`), `a` might exist but lack execute permission for you to traverse it (`EACCES` — you need execute, not read, permission on a directory to pass through it), `b` might exist but not be a directory (`ENOTDIR`), or `c.txt` genuinely doesn't exist in an otherwise-valid `b`.

**Correct model:** a path failure is about the *first broken link in the resolution chain*, not necessarily the final component. This is why `ls -la` on each intermediate directory, checking execute bits specifically, is the right debugging move for a mysterious "permission denied" on a file the owner insists exists.

slides.sectionTitle: Real numbers: how much a deep path actually costs
slides.markdown:
A cold resolution of `/a/b/c/d/e.txt` (5 components, nothing cached) costs roughly 5 directory-block reads plus 5 inode reads — on an HDD, at 5-10ms per random read, that's potentially 50-100ms just to open the file, before a single byte of its content is read. On a warm dentry and inode cache (the common case after the first access), the same resolution costs microseconds — pure in-memory hash lookups.

This gap is why applications that `stat()` or `open()` the same deep path in a tight loop see a dramatic speedup after the first call, and why container images with very deep, wide directory trees can show a slower "cold start" than flatter layouts.
